pqc_replacement.rationale: MD5 is broken by collision attacks. Replace unconditionally — not a PQC issue.
pqc_replacement.trade_offs: SHA-256 has negligible cost increase over MD5. No latency concern.

pqc_replacement.rationale: SHA-1 is deprecated for digital signatures. Legacy verification paths may continue temporarily.
pqc_replacement.trade_offs: SHA-256 produces 32-byte digest (vs 20). Storage impact minimal.

pqc_replacement.rationale: SHA-256 remains secure post-quantum. Grover's algorithm offers only quadratic speedup, absorbed by 256-bit output.
Grover's algorithm halves effective strength. AES-128 → 64-bit effective; AES-256 → 128-bit effective (safe).
pqc_replacement.trade_offs: AES-256 is ~40% slower than AES-128. On modern hardware with AES-NI, impact is negligible.

pqc_replacement.rationale: DES has a 56-bit key — broken classically. Replace with AES immediately.
pqc_replacement.trade_offs: AES is faster on modern hardware than DES.

pqc_replacement.rationale: RSA is broken by Shor's algorithm on a CRQC. Recommended migration: hybrid classical+PQC during transition (NIST IR 8547 protects hybrid deployment).
pqc_replacement.trade_offs: ML-KEM-768 public keys ~1.2 KB (vs RSA-2048 ~256 bytes). ML-DSA-65 signatures ~3.3 KB (vs RSA-2048 ~256 bytes). Expect larger handshakes and ~2× packet overhead in TLS. CPU cost higher — plan load-benchmarking before deployment.

pqc_replacement.rationale: ECDSA is broken by Shor's algorithm. FIPS 204 provides a drop-in PQC signature replacement.
pqc_replacement.trade_offs: ML-DSA-65 signatures larger (~3.3 KB vs ~70 bytes for ECDSA P-256). Consider bandwidth.

pqc_replacement.rationale: ECDH key exchange is Shor-vulnerable. Hybrid is recommended during transition to preserve backward compatibility.
pqc_replacement.trade_offs: ML-KEM-768 ciphertexts ~1 KB. TLS handshake grows by ~1-2 KB. Modern networks tolerate this easily.

pqc_replacement.rationale: ML-KEM is the NIST-standardized post-quantum KEM (formerly Kyber). No migration needed.
